title: Stop-Work Authority
why: Every person on this crew can stop work when something looks wrong. That includes the newest laborer. Most injuries on pipe jobs come after someone saw the problem and kept quiet.
key_points: Anyone can call a stop. You do not need to be the foreman or the competent person.
Call it out loud and clear: 'Stop, all stop.' Make sure the operator hears you or sees your signal.
Stopping work is not a write-up. Nobody on this job gets punished for calling a good-faith stop.
Once work stops, the foreman or competent person looks at the problem with you before anyone restarts.
Fix it, or change the plan. Work restarts only when the hazard is dealt with, not just talked about.
Federal law protects workers who raise safety concerns from retaliation (OSH Act Section 11(c)).
If you were wrong, that is fine. A false alarm costs five minutes. A missed one can cost a life.
ask: When was the last time you saw something and did not say anything? What stopped you?
What are the hand signals we use for 'stop' with the operator on this job?

quick_check.scenario: A new laborer sees a crack open up along the trench wall, about 3 ft back from the edge, while two guys are in the trench. He is not sure it matters and does not want to look stupid.
quick_check.answer: He calls 'All stop' and gets everyone out of the trench now. The competent person inspects before anyone goes back in. Cracks are a cave-in warning sign.

reference: 29 CFR 1926.21(b)(2) (training to recognize and avoid hazards)

title: Protective Systems: The 5-Foot Rule
why: A cubic yard of soil can weigh as much as a small car. When a trench wall lets go there is no time to climb out. Cave-ins kill pipelayers every year, and almost every one was in an unprotected trench. Fatal Four: caught-in/between — see TT-065.
key_points: A trench 5 ft or deeper needs a protective system: sloping, benching, shoring, or a shield (trench box). The only exception is a trench dug entirely in stable rock.
Under 5 ft, you still need protection if the competent person sees any sign of a possible cave-in.

20 ft or deeper: a registered professional engineer must design the system. OSHA's sloping and shoring tables (Appendices B, C and D) stop at 20 ft. Tabulated data, including a box manufacturer's data, counts only if a registered PE approved it for that depth.
Never enter an unprotected trench, not even 'for one second' to grab a tool or check grade.
Protection must be in place before anyone gets in, and stay in place until everyone is out.
Ask the competent person which system we are using today and why.
ask: How deep is our trench today and what is protecting us?
Where on this job are we tempted to step into an unprotected section?

quick_check.scenario: The trench is 4 ft 6 in deep in previously dug, sandy fill. The crew says it is under 5 ft so they don't need the box.
quick_check.answer: Wrong. Under 5 ft is only exempt if the competent person checks and finds no sign of a cave-in. Disturbed sandy fill is a red flag. The competent person decides, and protection goes in if there is any doubt.

reference: Subpart P Appendix B, Table B-1 note 3 (sloping or benching over 20 ft designed by a registered PE); Appendices C and D (scope: trenches not over 20 ft); 1926.650(b) (tabulated data is PE-approved)
California: Title 8 CCR 1539-1543 (excavations); Title 8 CCR 341(d)(5)(A) (Cal/OSHA permit for trenches 5 ft or deeper that anyone enters)

title: The Competent Person
why: OSHA puts one person on the hook for reading the ground every day: the competent person. If you do not know who that is on this job today, we have a problem before we dig. Fatal Four: caught-in/between — see TT-065.
key_points: The competent person can recognize existing and predictable hazards and has the authority to fix them right away.
They inspect the excavation, the area next to it, and the protective system daily, before work starts, and as needed through the shift.
They inspect again after every rainstorm or anything else that makes the trench more dangerous, like vibration, a water leak or new loads near the edge.
If they find signs of a cave-in, system failure, bad air or other hazard, everyone gets out until it is fixed.
They classify the soil and pick or approve the protective system based on it.
They monitor dewatering and check atmospheres where bad air could be expected.
If the competent person leaves the site, work in the trench stops or another competent person takes over. Know who it is.
ask: Who is our competent person today, and who covers if they leave?
What changes during a shift would make you ask for a re-inspection?

quick_check.scenario: At noon a water main leak starts seeping into the trench wall. The competent person inspected at 7 a.m. and went to another site.
quick_check.answer: Stop work and get out. Conditions changed, so a competent person must re-inspect before anyone re-enters. The morning check does not cover a new hazard.

title: Soil Types and Sloping
why: Different ground stands up differently. Sloping that works in hard clay can fail in sand. Your competent person classifies the soil so the protection matches the dirt you are actually in. Fatal Four: caught-in/between — see TT-065.
key_points: OSHA soil types are stable rock, Type A, Type B and Type C. Type A is strongest and Type C is weakest.
The competent person classifies soil using at least one visual and one manual test.
Previously disturbed soil (old trench lines, fill, around existing utilities) cannot be Type A.
Submerged soil, or soil with water freely seeping out of it, is Type C.

For excavations under 20 ft deep, OSHA's maximum allowable slopes are: Type A 3/4 to 1 (53 degrees), Type B 1 to 1 (45 degrees), Type C 1 1/2 to 1 (34 degrees). Deeper than 20 ft, a registered professional engineer designs the slope.
If the soil is not classified, slope as Type C at 1 1/2 to 1.
Layered soils: the weaker layer controls. Ground can change along the same trench; reclassify when it does.
Surcharge loads, vibration from traffic or equipment, and water can all downgrade the soil.
ask: What soil type did our competent person call today, and what tests were used?
Where on this alignment do we cross old trench lines or fill?

quick_check.scenario: You hit an old water line trench running across your cut. The rest of the trench is classified Type A.
quick_check.answer: The disturbed ground around that old line cannot be Type A. The competent person reclassifies, and the slope or system is adjusted for that section.

reference: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification)
29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix B (sloping and benching; Table B-1 and note 3)

title: Trench Boxes and Shoring
why: A box or shore only protects you if it is the right one, set the right way, and you stay inside it. Most box injuries happen when people step out past the end or ride it while it is being moved. Fatal Four: caught-in/between — see TT-065.
key_points: Use boxes and shores only within the manufacturer's tabulated data. A copy of the tabulated data must be kept on site.
Check the data plate and the tab data for the depth and soil type you are in. Do not stack boxes or add extensions unless the tab data allows it.
Nobody inside the box while it is being installed, removed, or moved vertically.
Work only inside the box. Stepping out the open end puts you in an unprotected trench.
The trench can be dug no more than 2 ft below the bottom of the shield, and only if the shield is rated for the full depth and no soil is running out from behind or below.
Backfill or block voids between the box and the trench wall so the box cannot shift sideways.

Inspect boxes, spreaders and hydraulic shores for damage, bent members and leaks. If the competent person cannot confirm damaged equipment is safe, it comes out of service until a registered professional engineer evaluates and approves it.
Install and remove hydraulic shores the way the manufacturer's instructions say. Removal starts at the bottom and works up, members are released slowly, and backfill follows as they come out.
ask: Where is the tabulated data for our box today?
What is the plan for getting pipe in without anyone stepping out of the box?

quick_check.scenario: The excavator is dragging the box forward and a pipelayer rides along inside to save time climbing out.
quick_check.answer: No. Nobody in the box while it is moved. He climbs out, the box gets moved and set, then he re-enters.

reference: 29 CFR 1926.652(e) (support systems; removal from the bottom, (e)(1)(v)-(vi))
Subpart P Appendices C and D

title: Spoil Piles and Edge Loads
why: Spoil, pipe and equipment near the edge do two things: they can fall on you, and their weight pushes on the trench wall. Edge loading is one of the most common setups for a cave-in. Fatal Four: caught-in/between and struck-by — see TT-065.
key_points: Keep spoil, materials and equipment at least 2 ft back from the edge, or use retaining devices that stop them rolling in.
2 ft is the minimum, not the target. Farther back is better, especially with heavy equipment or wet soil.
Do not stockpile pipe, structures or rock at the edge. Chock pipe so it cannot roll.
Keep trucks, loaders and the excavator tracks back from the edge unless the protective system is designed for that load.
Watch for rocks and clods rolling down the spoil pile into the trench. Scale or remove loose material.
Do not let the spoil pile block the ladder or the way out.
Place spoil on the side away from traffic and away from where people work, when you have the choice.
ask: Where are our heaviest loads sitting compared to the edge right now?
Who is watching the spoil pile while people are in the trench?

quick_check.scenario: Spoil is piled right at the lip on one side because the right-of-way is tight.
quick_check.answer: Not acceptable. Move it back at least 2 ft, haul some off, or use a retaining device. Get the competent person to check the wall for damage from the load.

title: Ladders and Egress
why: If the wall starts to move, water rushes in or the air goes bad, you have seconds to get out. The ladder has to be close, secured and clear before you need it. Fatal Four: caught-in/between and falls — see TT-065.
key_points: Trenches 4 ft or deeper need a ladder, stairway, ramp or other safe way out within 25 ft of lateral travel for every worker.
Long trenches or spread-out crews may need more than one ladder.
Keep the ladder inside the protected area, inside the box or shored section.
Ladder side rails extend at least 3 ft above the landing, and the ladder is secured so it cannot be knocked over.
Set the ladder on stable footing, not on loose spoil or pipe.
Face the ladder and keep your hands free. Do not carry tools or fittings up and down; hand them up or use a rope.
Move the ladder as the box moves. A ladder left back at the last setup does not count.
Never climb out on the box spreaders, the pipe, or the bucket.
ask: How far is the closest ladder from where you are working right now?
Who moves the ladder when we move the box?

quick_check.scenario: The box moves 30 ft down the trench. The ladder stays in the old spot.
quick_check.answer: Move the ladder into the box before anyone goes back in. Egress must be within 25 ft of travel, and it must be inside protection.

title: Water in the Trench
why: Water weakens soil fast, hides the bottom, and can undercut a trench wall in minutes. A trench that was fine at 7 a.m. can be dangerous after a rainstorm or a line break. Fatal Four: caught-in/between and electrocution — see TT-065.
key_points: Do not work in a trench with water accumulated or accumulating unless the precautions are in place: pumping, shoring or shields, or harness and lifeline, as the situation needs.
If pumps or wellpoints keep the water down, the competent person monitors them to make sure they keep working.
Divert surface water away from the trench with ditches, berms or dikes.
After rain or runoff, the competent person inspects before anyone goes back in.
Water freely seeping from the walls means the soil is Type C. Tell the competent person.
Watch for boiling or heave in the bottom. That is water pushing soil up and can undermine the box.
Gas-powered pumps in or near the trench give off carbon monoxide. Keep engines out of the trench and downwind.
Electric pumps need GFCI protection and cords kept out of the water where possible.
ask: What happens to our trench if the pump fails while we are at lunch?
Where does the water go when we discharge it?

quick_check.scenario: An overnight storm left 18 in of water in the trench. The foreman wants to pump it down and send the crew right in.
quick_check.answer: Pump it down, then the competent person inspects the walls, the box and the bottom before anyone enters. Rain is a hazard-increasing event that requires inspection.

title: Warning Signs of a Cave-In
why: The ground usually warns you before it fails. The crew up top often sees it before the people in the hole. Learn the signs and get people out the moment you see one. Fatal Four: caught-in/between — see TT-065.
key_points: Tension cracks running parallel to the trench on the surface, usually back from the edge.
Chunks or dirt falling off the wall, called sloughing or spalling.
Bulging or bellying of the trench wall.
Water seeping out of the wall or pooling at the bottom.
Soil running out from under or behind the box, or the box shifting.
Bottom heaving or boiling up.
Shoring members bending, popping or leaking hydraulic fluid.
When you see any of these: get everyone out, keep people and equipment away from the edge, and call the competent person.
ask: Which of these signs have you seen on a job before? What happened?
Who has the best view of the walls when the excavator is digging?

quick_check.scenario: From the spoil side, the operator sees a crack opening about 4 ft back from the edge. He thinks it's just drying out.
quick_check.answer: Stop and get everyone out of the trench. Cracks parallel to the trench are a classic warning sign. The competent person inspects and decides on the fix.

title: Laying Pipe in the Box
why: The pipelayer's job puts you right where the load, the bucket and the trench wall all meet. Most pipelaying injuries are crushed hands and feet, or getting caught between the pipe and the box. Fatal Four: caught-in/between and struck-by — see TT-065.
key_points: Stay inside the box when pipe is lowered. Step to the side of the opening, never directly under the load.
Guide pipe with tag lines or by hand on the outside of the pipe, never with your fingers in the bell or between pipe and box.
When the excavator pushes pipe home with the bucket, use the method the pipe manufacturer allows (such as a timber between bucket and pipe), and keep hands and feet clear of the joint.
Keep your feet out from under the pipe until it is down, bedded and stable.
Lubricate and check the gasket before making the joint, not while the pipe is moving.
Watch for the pipe rolling or kicking when the sling is released.
One person gives signals to the operator. Everyone else stays quiet on the radio or hands.
Keep the bottom clean so you are not tripping over bedding piles and fittings.
ask: Where do you put your hands when a joint is being pushed home?
How do we know when it is safe to unhook the sling?

quick_check.scenario: While pushing a joint home, the pipelayer reaches in to straighten the gasket as the pipe moves.
quick_check.answer: No. Signal the operator to stop, wait for the pipe to stop moving, then fix the gasket. Hands never go into the joint while anything is moving.

title: Call 811 and Read the Marks
why: Hitting a gas line or a power line can kill the whole crew, not just the operator. A locate ticket is the first line of defense, but only if we read the marks and respect them. Fatal Four: electrocution — see TT-065.
key_points: Locates must be requested before digging. Call 811 or use your state's online system, and wait the time your state requires.
Check the ticket before you dig: right address, right limits, not expired, and every utility has responded.
White paint or flags mark where we plan to dig, where your state uses white-lining.

APWA colors: red electric, yellow gas/oil/steam, orange communications, blue potable water, green sewer/storm drain, purple reclaimed water/irrigation/slurry, pink temporary survey, white proposed excavation.
Marks show approximate location only. The line can be anywhere inside your state's tolerance zone on either side of the mark.
Look for things the marks do not show: meters, valve boxes, manholes, pedestals, risers, patch lines in the pavement. Unmarked does not mean nothing is there.
Private lines (service laterals, irrigation, site lighting) are often not located by 811. Ask the owner or use a private locator.
If marks are missing, faded or wrong, stop and call for a re-mark.
ask: What is our ticket number and when does it expire?
What is on this job that 811 will not locate?

quick_check.scenario: You see a gas meter on the house but there is no yellow paint in the front yard.
quick_check.answer: Do not dig. The service line is probably there. Call in for a re-mark or emergency locate and wait for it. Treat it as live until proven otherwise.

reference: California: Title 8 CCR 1541(b) and Government Code 4216 (notify the regional notification center at least 2 working days before digging)

title: Potholing and Hand Digging
why: Locate paint tells you where a line probably is. Potholing tells you where it actually is. Exposing the line before the bucket gets close is how we avoid strikes. Fatal Four: electrocution — see TT-065.
key_points: When the dig approaches a marked utility, find the exact location by safe means: hand digging, vacuum excavation, or other methods your state allows.
Inside the tolerance zone, no mechanical digging unless your state law and the facility owner allow it. Know your state's tolerance zone width.
Pothole at every crossing and at enough points along a parallel line to know where it runs.
Hand tools: use a blunt or rounded shovel, pry soil sideways, do not stab or spike straight down onto a line.
Vacuum excavation: follow the equipment's pressure limits and keep the wand moving so you don't cut a coating or cable.
Once exposed, support and protect the line. Do not let it hang unsupported or use it as a step.
Mark the exposed depth so the operator knows exactly where it is.
Report any damage, even a scratch or dent in a coating. A nicked gas line can fail later.
ask: How close does the bucket get to a mark on this job before we switch to hand digging or vac?
Who tells the operator the line is exposed?

quick_check.scenario: You scrape the coating on a steel gas line while potholing. It is not leaking.
quick_check.answer: Stop and call the gas company right away. Coating damage must be reported and repaired. Do not backfill over it.

title: Utility Strike Response
why: Even with good locates, strikes happen. What the crew does in the first minute decides whether a damaged line becomes a fire, an explosion, or an electrocution. Fatal Four: electrocution — see TT-065.
key_points: Gas strike: stop, shut down equipment only if you can do it safely and quickly, and get everyone out, upwind and well away.
No ignition sources near a gas leak: no smoking, no starting engines, no phones or radios close to the leak.
Call 911, then the gas company. Do not try to crimp, plug or bury a leaking gas line.
Keep the public and traffic away until the fire department or utility takes over.
Electric strike: if you are in the machine, stay in the cab unless there is a fire. Warn everyone to stay away from the machine and the ground near it.
If you must leave an energized machine because of fire, jump clear with feet together without touching the machine and ground at the same time, then shuffle away with feet together.
Water main or sewer strike: get people out of the trench, as water can undercut walls fast. Call the owner to shut it down.
Report every strike, even a nick. Take photos, keep the area as it was, and tell the foreman.
ask: Where do we go if we hit gas on this job? Which way is the wind today?
Who has the utility emergency numbers?

quick_check.scenario: The excavator hooks a buried power cable and sparks fly. A laborer starts to walk over to look.
quick_check.answer: Yell to stop him and keep everyone away. The machine and the ground around it may be energized. The operator stays in the cab unless there is a fire, and the crew calls 911 and the electric utility.

reference: OSHA FS-3941 (equipment contact with power lines)

title: Overhead Power Lines
why: An excavator boom, a dump bed or a pipe swinging on a sling can reach a power line without the operator ever seeing it. Electricity can jump the gap, and the people touching the machine get hurt worst. Fatal Four: electrocution — see TT-065.
key_points: Look up before you set up. Walk the site and point out every overhead line to the crew and operators.
For lines rated 50 kV or less, keep equipment at least 10 ft away. Higher voltage needs more clearance. Treat every line as energized unless the utility confirms it is de-energized and grounded.
If you don't know the voltage, call the utility. Do not guess.
Use a dedicated spotter whenever equipment could get close to the minimum distance.
Raise dump beds only clear of lines. Lower them before moving.
Watch the load and the slings, not only the boom. A swinging pipe can bring the line to you.
If equipment contacts a line, follow the strike response: operator stays in the cab unless there is a fire, everyone else stays clear.
Ask about de-energizing or insulating the line when the work has to be close.
ask: Where are the overhead lines on this job, and who spots when we work under them?
What equipment on this site can reach the lines?

quick_check.scenario: A dump truck driver raises the bed to dump bedding rock right under a service drop.
quick_check.answer: Stop. Move the truck clear of the line before raising the bed, with a spotter watching.

reference: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC (1926.1407-1411) for boom trucks or cranes unloading or setting pipe and structures; excavators lifting with rigging are excluded (1926.1400(c)(2))
OSHA FS-3941 (equipment contact: stay in the cab, jump clear, shuffle)

title: Working Next to Live Sewer and Water Lines
why: Tie-ins and work beside live lines expose us to sewage, high-pressure water and sudden flooding. A failed plug or a cracked old main can fill a trench in seconds. Fatal Four: caught-in/between and struck-by — see TT-065.
key_points: Treat every existing line as live until the owner confirms it is shut down and drained.
Old pipe is brittle. Asbestos-cement, clay and old cast iron can crack when disturbed. Support exposed lines and keep equipment off them.
Know where the shut-off valves are and who can operate them before you cut into a water main.
Live sewer: wear gloves and eye protection, wash hands before eating, drinking or smoking, and keep cuts covered.
Keep your tetanus shot up to date, and ask your doctor about other vaccines for sewage work.
Plugs and bypasses must be installed and checked per the plan. Never stand in line with a plug that is holding back flow.
Have an exit plan. If a plug or main fails, everyone out of the trench immediately.
Asbestos-cement pipe: do not cut, break or grind it unless you are trained and following the company's asbestos procedure.
ask: Who has the valve key and the owner's contact for this tie-in?
What is our plan if the plug fails?

quick_check.scenario: Cutting into a sewer for a tie-in, the crew finds the pipe is old asbestos-cement, not PVC like the plans said.
quick_check.answer: Stop cutting. Asbestos-cement requires trained workers and specific methods. Call the foreman and follow the company's asbestos procedure before continuing.

reference: CDC: Reducing health risks to workers handling human waste or sewage

title: Confined Spaces on Our Jobs
why: Manholes, wet wells, vaults, lift stations and large pipe are confined spaces. People die in them from bad air they cannot see or smell, and too often it is the rescuer who goes in after them.
key_points: A confined space is big enough to enter, has limited ways in or out, and is not designed for continuous occupancy.
A permit-required space has, or could have, a hazardous atmosphere, engulfment, an inward-converging shape that can trap you, or another serious hazard.
Most manholes and wet wells on sewer jobs should be treated as permit spaces until the competent person evaluates them.
Before entry: permit filled out and posted, air tested, ventilation running, attendant in place, rescue plan ready.
Never enter a permit space without the permit and an attendant, even just to grab a tool or read a laser.
The space can change. New pipe connections, flow, pumps running nearby or hot work can all change the air.
Construction confined spaces are covered by 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA. Know who our competent person and entry supervisor are.
Fill out a permit for every entry: on paper or in The Pipelayer's Bible. The entry supervisor decides if entry is safe.
ask: Which spaces on this job are permit spaces?
Who is the entry supervisor today?

quick_check.scenario: A laborer wants to climb into a new manhole for a minute to check the invert. Nothing is connected yet, so he says it's safe.
quick_check.answer: No entry without evaluation. The competent person checks the space, and if it is a permit space, the full permit process is followed: test, ventilate, attendant, rescue plan.

reference: California: Title 8 CCR 1950-1962 (confined spaces in construction)

title: Atmospheric Testing
why: You cannot see, smell or taste most of the gases that kill people in manholes and trenches. The gas monitor is the only thing that tells you the truth, and only if it works and you use it right.
key_points: Test before entry, from outside the space, using a calibrated monitor.
Test in this order: oxygen first, then flammable gases, then toxic gases like H2S and CO.
Test at the top, middle and bottom. Some gases are heavier than air and sit low; some are lighter and rise.
A hazardous atmosphere includes oxygen below 19.5% or above 23.5%, or flammable gas over 10% of the lower flammable limit (LFL/LEL).
Bump test the monitor before each day's use per the manufacturer, and keep it calibrated.
Keep monitoring during entry. Conditions change when flow starts or work begins.
Excavations over 4 ft deep where bad air could be expected (landfills, near fuel tanks, near sewers) must be tested before entry.
If the alarm goes off, everyone out now. Do not wait to see if it clears.
ask: When was our gas monitor last bump tested? Calibrated?
Why do we test oxygen first?

quick_check.scenario: The monitor reads fine at the top of a manhole. The entrant wants to go in without lowering the sensor.
quick_check.answer: No. Lower the sensor and test all levels before entry. Heavy gases like H2S can sit at the bottom while the top reads clean.

reference: OSHA SHIB: Calibrating and Testing Direct-Reading Portable Gas Monitors (bump test before each day's use)

title: Hydrogen Sulfide and Sewer Gas
why: H2S forms wherever sewage sits and rots. At low levels it smells like rotten eggs. At higher levels it kills your sense of smell, so the danger seems to go away just as it gets worse.
key_points: H2S is heavier than air. It collects in manholes, wet wells, low spots and trenches near sewers.
Never trust your nose. Loss of the smell can mean the level went up, not down.
Disturbing sewage (pumping, bypassing, breaking into a line) can release a burst of H2S.
Sewers also hold methane (flammable) and can be short on oxygen. Test for all of them.
Ventilate the space and keep monitoring. Wear a personal H2S or 4-gas monitor in the breathing zone.
Symptoms include eye irritation, headache, nausea and dizziness. At high levels it can knock you down in seconds.
If someone collapses, do not go in after them without rescue equipment and training. Call for rescue.
Follow the monitor's alarm settings and your permit. Do not override or silence alarms.
ask: What does the H2S alarm sound like on our monitors?
Where on this job could sewer gas build up outside a manhole?

quick_check.scenario: The crew smells rotten eggs at a manhole. After a few minutes nobody smells it any more.
quick_check.answer: That is a warning, not an all-clear. H2S can deaden your smell. Get away, test with a monitor, and ventilate before anyone enters.

title: Attendants and Rescue
why: Many confined space deaths are would-be rescuers. They see a buddy go down and jump in. The attendant's job is to stay out and get help.
key_points: The attendant stays outside the space for the whole entry and keeps count of who is inside.
The attendant keeps in contact with the entrants and watches for changes inside and outside the space.
The attendant orders everyone out if the monitor alarms, conditions change, or an entrant acts strangely.
The attendant never enters to rescue unless relieved by another attendant and trained and equipped for rescue.
Use non-entry rescue first: harness, retrieval line and a tripod and winch. A mechanical retrieval device is required for vertical spaces deeper than 5 ft.
Know who the rescue service is, how to call them, and how long they take to arrive, before entry starts.
Keep unauthorized people away from the opening.
Practice the rescue. A plan nobody has tried is a guess.
ask: Who is the rescue service for this job, and how do we call them?
What does the attendant do if the entrant stops answering?

quick_check.scenario: The entrant stops answering. The attendant's first instinct is to climb down the ladder.
quick_check.answer: No. The attendant calls for rescue, tries to retrieve with the line and winch from outside, and does not enter. Going in makes two victims.

reference: 29 CFR 1926.1211 (rescue and emergency services; (c)(2) mechanical retrieval over 5 ft)

title: Struck-By: Excavators and Loaders
why: On pipe jobs, the excavator and loader are always moving near people on foot. An operator can lose sight of you in a second. Being struck by equipment is one of the top killers in construction. Fatal Four: struck-by — see TT-065.
key_points: Make eye contact with the operator before you walk into their work area. If they cannot see you, assume they don't know you are there.
Stay out of blind spots: behind the machine, right beside the tracks, and under or near the bucket.
Nobody under a load handled by lifting or digging equipment. Ever.
Stand clear of trucks being loaded so spillage or falling material can't hit you.
Wear high-visibility clothing near equipment and traffic.
Operators: sound the horn before moving, and stop if someone walks into your area unexpectedly.
Loaders carrying pipe or material: travel with the bucket or forks low, watch for people on foot, and slow down in tight areas.
Plan walking routes that keep the crew away from the machine's travel path.
ask: Where are the blind spots on the machines we have on site today?
How do you get the operator's attention safely?

quick_check.scenario: A laborer walks behind the excavator to grab a shovel while the operator is swinging to dump.
quick_check.answer: Never cross behind a working machine. Get the operator's attention, wait for the signal to approach, then go.

title: Swing Radius and Spotters
why: The back end of an excavator swings with enough force to crush a person against a truck, a wall or a trench box. The operator is often looking at the bucket, not the counterweight. Fatal Four: struck-by and caught-in/between — see TT-065.
key_points: Mark the swing radius with cones, tape or barricades where people could walk into it.
Nobody enters the swing radius without making eye contact with the operator and getting a clear signal.
Never stand between the counterweight and a fixed object: a truck, pipe stack, wall or another machine.
Use a spotter when the operator's view is blocked, when working near traffic, power lines, or people.
The spotter watches the machine, stays in the operator's view, and stays out of the swing radius and line of travel.
Agree on hand signals before work starts. One person signals at a time. Anyone can give a stop signal.
If the operator loses sight of the spotter, the machine stops.
Spotters don't do other work at the same time. Watching the machine is the job.
ask: Show me our stop signal and our 'come ahead' signal.
Where on this site does the swing radius come close to a truck or fixed object?

quick_check.scenario: The spotter steps behind a dump truck to get a better view and drops out of the operator's sight.
quick_check.answer: The operator stops all movement until the spotter is back in view. No eyes on the spotter means no movement.

title: Backing and Dump Trucks
why: Backing vehicles cause a large share of struck-by deaths in work zones. Dump trucks hauling bedding and spoil back up all day, often into the same area where people are working. Fatal Four: struck-by — see TT-065.
key_points: Vehicles with an obstructed rear view must not back up unless they have a working backup alarm audible above surrounding noise, or a spotter signals that it is safe.
Backup alarms are not enough by themselves. People get used to them. Use a spotter in tight or busy areas.
Drivers: if you lose sight of the spotter, stop.
Spotters stand where the driver can see them in the mirror, never directly behind the truck.
Plan the site so trucks back up as little as possible. Pull-through routes are best.
Keep foot traffic out of truck staging and dump areas.
Walk around the vehicle before you back up if you've been parked.
Dump beds come down before the truck moves.
ask: Where is the truck route and turnaround today?
Who spots the trucks when we're backfilling?

quick_check.scenario: The backup alarm on a dump truck stopped working this morning. The driver says he'll just be careful.
quick_check.answer: That truck does not back up without a spotter until the alarm is fixed. Report it to the foreman.

title: Line of Fire
why: Line of fire means putting your body in the path of something that can move, fall, swing, spray or snap. On a pipe job that is suspended pipe, a swinging bucket, a pressurized hose, or a cable under tension. Fatal Four: struck-by and caught-in/between — see TT-065.
key_points: Before every task ask: what could move, and where would it go? Then stand somewhere else.
Suspended loads: never under, and not in the path if it swings or drops.
Pressurized lines: test plugs, pump hoses and hydraulic lines can release with deadly force. Stay out of line with them.
Cables, chains and come-alongs under tension can snap back. Stand to the side.
Rolling or falling objects: pipe on a slope, unchocked pipe, rock on the spoil pile.
Moving equipment: the path of the machine, the swing of the counterweight, the travel of a backing truck.
Flying debris from saws, grinders and hammers: know where the material is going.
If you notice someone in the line of fire, tell them. That's what a crew does.
ask: What's one task today where someone could end up in the line of fire?
Where do you stand when a pipe plug is under pressure?

quick_check.scenario: A laborer stands in front of the pipe end while the operator pulls a sling free from under a joint.
quick_check.answer: Move to the side. The sling can whip out and the pipe can roll. Stand clear of the path before the operator pulls.

title: Pinch Points and Caught-Between
why: Hands and fingers get crushed every day on pipe jobs: between pipe joints, between pipe and box, in rigging, on tailgates and in machine linkages. A caught-between incident with equipment can kill. Fatal Four: caught-in/between — see TT-065.
key_points: Identify the pinch points before you start: pipe joints, bells, slings, quick couplers, tailgates, box spreaders, trailer ramps.
Keep your hands on the outside of the load. Use tag lines, push sticks or tools to guide pipe.
Never put your hands where you can't see them.
Do not stand between a moving machine and a fixed object: wall, truck, pipe stack or trench box.
Stay out of the articulation point of loaders and the swing area of excavators.
Gloves help with cuts, not crushing. Gloves don't make it okay to put your hand in a pinch point.
Equipment linkages and attachments: lower to the ground and shut down before anyone works near them.
Wear rings? Take them off. Loose clothing and long hair can get caught in rotating parts.
ask: Where are the pinch points on the task we're doing today?
What tools do we have so nobody has to use their hands to guide pipe?

quick_check.scenario: A laborer holds the bucket teeth to steady them while the operator lines up a quick coupler pin.
quick_check.answer: Never. Hands off. Operator lowers the attachment, shuts down if needed, and the pin gets lined up with a tool.

title: Lockout, Tagout and Blocking
why: Machines and pumps can start, move or release stored energy while someone is working on them. Hydraulics hold buckets in the air, and a pump can be started by someone who didn't know you were in the line. Fatal Four: caught-in/between and electrocution — see TT-065.
key_points: Before working on equipment: lower the bucket or blade to the ground, set the brake, shut off the engine and take the key.
Lock and tag the controls or disconnect per the company's lockout program. Your lock, your key.
Bleed off stored energy: hydraulic pressure, air pressure, springs and trapped water in lines.
Anything held up must be blocked before you work under or between it. Do not trust hydraulics.
Blades, buckets and dump bodies must be fully lowered or blocked when being repaired or not in use.
Pumps and bypass systems: lock out before working on the pump, hoses or lines it feeds.
Electrical circuits: lock out and tag before working on them, and test to verify they are dead.
Try the start before you begin work to verify the energy is off, then put the controls back in neutral or off.
ask: What equipment on this job has stored energy we might forget about?
Where are the locks and tags kept?

quick_check.scenario: A mechanic needs to change a hose on the excavator boom. The bucket is in the air because it's easier to reach.
quick_check.answer: Lower the bucket to the ground or block it securely first, shut down and lock out. Nobody works under a raised attachment held only by hydraulics.

reference: 29 CFR 1910.147 (general industry; used as best practice reference)

title: Lifting and Lowering Pipe with the Excavator
why: On a pipe job the excavator is the crane. Every stick goes from the stack, over the spoil and down into the box on a sling. A dropped or swinging pipe in a trench has nowhere to go but onto the pipelayer. Fatal Four: struck-by and caught-in/between — see TT-065.
key_points: Lift only from the rated lifting hook or lifting eye the manufacturer put on the bucket linkage or coupler. Never hang a sling from bucket teeth or the bucket lip.
Know the weight, and check the machine's lifting capacity chart at that reach. Capacity drops as the boom reaches out.
Choker hitch: choke on the sling body near the balance point, never on a splice or fitting, and use the tag's choker rating. Basket hitch: balance the load so it can't slide out.
Long sticks and fused pipe: use a spreader bar so the pipe stays level.
Coated, lined and plastic pipe: use nylon or wide fabric slings, not chains, wire rope or bare hooks. Pad any hook used in a pipe end.
Use a tag line to steady the pipe. Never grab a swinging load. "No employee shall be permitted underneath loads handled by lifting or digging equipment."
Lowering into the box: pipelayers stay inside the box, clear of the opening, until the pipe is low and steady. Never push pipe off the bank or drop it in.
One pipelayer signals the operator, with signals agreed before the first stick. If the operator loses sight of him or the signal isn't clear, the load stops.
ask: Where is the rated lift point on our machine, and what does the chart say at today's reach?
Which slings do we use on this pipe, and why not the chain?

quick_check.scenario: The operator hooks a choker around one bucket tooth to lift a joint of ductile pipe.
quick_check.answer: No. Teeth are not a lifting point. Use the excavator's designated lift point and rated rigging, and check the lift chart for the weight.

reference: 29 CFR 1926.251(a) and (e) (rigging; markings and rated capacity by hitch)
29 CFR 1926.1400(c)(2) (excavators lifting with rigging are outside Subpart CC; follow the manufacturer)
DIPRA, Installation Guide for Ductile Iron Pipe (2015), Sec. 1.4-1.5 and 3.3
Plastics Pipe Institute, Pipe Handling Accessories (HDPE)

title: Slings and Rigging Inspection
why: Slings wear out from cuts, heat, chemicals and sharp pipe edges. A sling that fails drops the load all at once. Inspection takes a minute; it's the only warning you'll get. Fatal Four: struck-by — see TT-065.
key_points: Slings and fittings are inspected each day before use by a competent person. Damaged rigging comes out of service right away.
Every sling needs a readable tag showing its rated capacity. OSHA does not allow rigging to be used without legible identification markings. No tag, no use.
Nylon and web slings for pipe: remove if you see cuts, tears, punctures, snags, acid or caustic burns, melting or charring, broken or worn stitching, or distorted fittings.
Chains and wire rope for precast and heavy fittings: look for broken wires, kinks, crushing, stretched or cracked links and hooks, and heat damage.
Go by the tag for the hitch you are using: vertical, choker or basket. Capacity also drops as sling legs get flatter.
Pad slings at sharp edges: cut pipe ends, bevels, precast edges and lifting hardware.
Never tie knots in a sling or shorten it by twisting.
Rigging not in use comes out of the work area. Store slings off the ground and out of sun, chemicals and heat.
ask: Where do damaged slings go on this job so nobody grabs them by mistake?
How does a choker hitch change a sling's capacity?

quick_check.scenario: A web sling has a small cut along the edge, but the tag is still readable and the load is light.
quick_check.answer: Take it out of service. Cuts are a removal criterion no matter how light the load is. Use a good sling.

reference: 29 CFR 1926.251(a) (general rigging requirements; (a)(2) markings; (a)(3) idle rigging removed; (a)(6) daily inspection)
29 CFR 1926.251(c)(9) (pad or protect slings from sharp edges)
OSHA Guidance on Safe Sling Use

title: Lifting by Hand
why: Back, shoulder and knee injuries from lifting fittings, plugs, hand tools and short pipe can end a career just as surely as a big accident. They often build up quietly over years.
key_points: Size up the load before you lift. Check the weight, the grip and the path, and look for anything in the way.
If it's too heavy or awkward, get help or use equipment. No prize for being the guy who lifts it alone.
Lift with your legs, keep the load close to your body, and don't twist. Turn with your feet.
Footing in the trench is uneven and wet. Get a solid stance before you lift.
Hand fittings and tools down into the trench, or lower them with a rope or the machine. Don't climb a ladder carrying them.
Team lifts: one person calls the lift, everyone lifts and sets down together.
Watch for pinch points when setting the load down.
Report strains early. Small problems become big ones if you keep working on them.
ask: What's the heaviest item we lift by hand on this job? Should we?
Where can we use the machine instead of muscle this week?

quick_check.scenario: A worker grabs a 12-inch fitting off the truck by himself and twists to toss it down the trench.
quick_check.answer: Get help or use the machine, lift close with your legs, turn with your feet, and lower it into the trench. Never toss material to someone in a trench.

reference: OSHA General Duty Clause (OSH Act Section 5(a)(1))

title: Pipe Lasers
why: Pipe and rotating lasers are on every grade job. They can damage eyes, and setting them up often puts people in manholes and trenches where other hazards are waiting.
key_points: Only trained, qualified people install, adjust and operate the laser, and the operator carries proof of qualification.
Never look into the beam or point it at anyone. Never use your eye to align the laser; use the target or a detector.
Post laser warning placards where lasers are used.
Cap the beam or turn the laser off when it's not needed, and when it will be unattended for a long time.
Setting a pipe laser in a manhole means confined space entry rules apply. Test, permit and attendant first.
Setting or checking a laser in the trench means protection must be in place. No 'quick' trips into an open cut.
Protect the laser from the bucket and falling material. If it gets bumped, re-check it before use.
Follow the manufacturer's manual and the laser's class label.
ask: Who is trained to set up the laser on this crew?
Where does the laser sit, and does setting it put anyone in a manhole or unprotected trench?

quick_check.scenario: Someone looks down the pipe to see if the laser is lined up on the target.
quick_check.answer: Don't look into the beam. Use the target or detector to check alignment, and keep eyes out of the beam path.

title: Grade Checking at the Trench
why: The grade checker spends the day right next to the bucket and the trench edge. Checking grade is where people step into unprotected trenches and walk into the swing radius. Fatal Four: caught-in/between and struck-by — see TT-065.
key_points: Check grade from inside the protected area or from outside the trench. Never step into an unprotected section to set a rod.
Make eye contact with the operator and agree on signals before going near the bucket.
The bucket stops before you put a rod, tape or hand near it. No checking while it moves.
Stay out of the swing radius except when the operator knows you are there and has stopped.
Keep your tripod and gear back from the edge (at least 2 ft, like any equipment). Your weight loads the edge too.
Machine control and GPS systems: keep people clear while the operator is focused on the screen.
Watch your footing on spoil, mud and uneven ground.
Wear high-visibility gear. You are often the person closest to the machine.
ask: What signal do we use for 'stop, I'm checking grade'?
Where can you check grade without leaving protection?

quick_check.scenario: The grade checker steps into the trench ahead of the box to shoot the bottom.
quick_check.answer: No. Ahead of the box is unprotected trench. Check from inside the box or from the surface with a rod and laser receiver.

title: Work Zone Setup
why: Drivers are distracted, speeding or don't see us. The traffic control setup is the wall between our crew and a car going 45 mph. A sloppy setup gets people killed. Fatal Four: struck-by — see TT-065.
key_points: Traffic control follows the approved traffic control plan and the MUTCD Part 6. Don't freelance the layout.
Set up in the order the plan calls for, usually advance warning signs first, then the taper, then the work area. Take it down in reverse.
Set signs and cones facing traffic, in the direction the driver will see them first.
Keep the buffer space clear. No parked trucks, pipe or spoil in the buffer.
Check the setup during the day. Cones get knocked over, signs get turned, and conditions change.
Adjust for night work, curves and hills where drivers can't see the work zone in time.
Pedestrians and sidewalks need a safe, accessible route too, not just cars.
Only trained people set up and maintain traffic control. Follow the plan your agency approved.
ask: Who is responsible for checking our traffic control today?
What happens to the setup when we move down the street?

quick_check.scenario: Halfway through the day, a truck knocked down three cones in the taper.
quick_check.answer: Reset the taper right away, from a safe position, using the approach the plan calls for. A broken taper funnels traffic into the work area.

reference: 29 CFR 1926.200-203 (Subpart G signs, signals and barricades)
California: California MUTCD (Caltrans), which replaces the national MUTCD on California jobs

title: Flagging
why: The flagger stands in the road and controls traffic with a paddle. It is one of the most dangerous jobs on the site and needs the right training, the right gear and full attention. Fatal Four: struck-by — see TT-065.
key_points: Only trained flaggers on our jobs. The MUTCD calls for flagger training, and many states require certification.
Use a STOP/SLOW paddle as your primary device. Hand signals follow the MUTCD.
Wear high-visibility safety apparel meeting ANSI/ISEA 107 Performance Class 2 or 3, day and night. Consider Class 3 at night.
Stand on the shoulder or in the closed lane. Step into the traffic lane only after traffic has stopped. Have an escape route planned.
Face traffic. Never turn your back on oncoming cars.
Stay alert. No phones, no sitting, no headphones while flagging.
Make sure the flagger station is visible from far enough away, with advance warning signs.
Flaggers communicate with each other by radio or sight. Agree on how before you start.
ask: Where is the flagger's escape route today?
What do you do if a driver ignores your STOP paddle?

quick_check.scenario: A flagger stands in the middle of the open lane to make sure drivers see him.
quick_check.answer: Move to the shoulder or the closed lane. Stay visible but out of the travel path, with an escape route ready.

title: Working Beside Live Traffic
why: Our trenches are often right beside traffic. A car can come through the cones, or a driver can clip someone stepping out of the work zone to grab material. Fatal Four: struck-by — see TT-065.
key_points: Everyone exposed to traffic wears a high-visibility vest or garment. No exceptions, even for a minute.
Stay inside the work zone. Don't step outside the cones to grab tools or material.
Face traffic when you can. If you can't, have someone watch for you.
Enter and exit equipment on the side away from traffic.
Park personal vehicles out of the work zone and away from the traffic side.
Night work: wear the right reflective gear and keep lights aimed so they don't blind drivers.
Have an escape plan. Know where you'd go if a car came through.
Report near misses with traffic. They tell us the setup needs to change.
ask: Where would you go if a car came through our cones right now?
What makes drivers ignore our setup on this road?

quick_check.scenario: A laborer steps out between the cones to grab a shovel off the truck parked on the traffic side.
quick_check.answer: Stay in the zone. Trucks with tools should be parked inside the work area or on the protected side. Walk around through the work area to get there.

title: Silica: Cutting Concrete and Asphalt
why: Cutting concrete pavement, curb, concrete pipe and manholes throws fine silica dust. Breathe it for years and it scars your lungs (silicosis), which does not heal, and it also causes lung cancer and kidney disease.
key_points: Silica dust comes from concrete, asphalt with aggregate, brick, block, rock and concrete pipe. PVC doesn't contain silica, but most ductile iron pipe has a cement-mortar lining that does.
The OSHA permissible exposure limit is 50 micrograms per cubic meter averaged over 8 hours. The action level is 25.
Use water. Under Table 1 of the silica standard, cut-off saws need a built-in water system feeding the blade nonstop. Jackhammers need water at the point of impact, or a shroud with a dust collector.
Follow Table 1 for your exact task: controls and respirator needs depend on the tool, indoors or outdoors, and how long you cut.
Don't dry sweep or blow off with compressed air when it makes dust. Use water or a HEPA vacuum.
The company must have a written exposure control plan and a competent person to carry it out.
Workers required to wear a respirator 30 or more days a year must be offered medical exams.
If a respirator is required, you need fit testing and a clean shave where the seal touches your face.
ask: What tools on this job make silica dust?
Is the water on our saw working right now?

quick_check.scenario: The water tank on the cut-off saw is empty. The operator says he'll just cut the last few feet dry.
quick_check.answer: No dry cutting. Refill the water and get it flowing to the blade first. Table 1 controls must be working.

title: Carbon Monoxide
why: Gas-powered pumps, saws, generators and compactors make carbon monoxide. In a trench, manhole or vault, CO collects with nowhere to go. You can't see or smell it, and it can knock you out.
key_points: CO comes from gas and diesel engines. Small gasoline engines on pumps, saws, tampers and generators put out high levels.
Never run engines inside a trench, manhole, vault or other confined area unless air is monitored and controlled.
Place pumps, generators and compressors outside the trench and downwind.
Gas-powered tampers and saws in the trench can build up CO quickly. Monitor the air, or use electric or air-powered tools where you can.
Symptoms include headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion and tiredness. Often it feels like the flu.
If someone shows symptoms, get them to fresh air and call for help.
Wear a CO monitor when using engines near confined areas.
Ventilate when needed, and remember fans can also blow exhaust in if set up wrong.
ask: Where are we running engines near trenches or manholes today?
What are the early signs of CO poisoning?

quick_check.scenario: A worker using a gas tamper in a deep trench gets a headache and feels dizzy.
quick_check.answer: Shut off the tamper, get him out to fresh air, test the trench air, and call for help if symptoms don't clear. Don't continue until CO is controlled.

reference: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA (if in a confined space)
NIOSH 96-118 (CO from small gasoline engines and tools)

title: Heat Illness
why: Heat kills construction workers every summer. Heat stroke can kill fast, and new workers and people coming back from time off are at highest risk.
key_points: Drink water often, before you feel thirsty. About 1 cup every 15 to 20 minutes beats a lot at once.
Take rest breaks in shade or a cool place, more often on hot days or during heavy work.

State heat rules (follow the strictest you work under): at least 1 quart of water per person per hour for the whole shift; shade up from 80°F (from 52°F in nonbreathable suits in Washington); high-heat steps from 90°F (Washington, Oregon, Maryland) or 95°F (California): watch each other, check in by radio, pre-shift reminder; rest at least 10 minutes every 2 hours from 90°F and 15 minutes every hour from 100°F (Washington, Maryland); anyone who asks gets a cool-down rest of at least 5 minutes in the shade (California); a new worker is watched closely for the first 14 days.

New and returning workers need time to get used to heat. NIOSH: new workers start at no more than 20% of a full day's heat exposure and add no more than 20% a day; returning workers go 50%, 60%, 80%, then 100%.
Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea, headache. Stop work, cool down, drink water, and get help if it doesn't improve.
Heat stroke: confusion, slurred speech, passing out, seizures, very high body temperature, skin may be hot and dry or still sweating. Call 911.
For heat stroke, cool the person right away: shade, remove extra clothing, soak with water and fan, and ice on the neck, armpits and groin while waiting for help.
Watch your buddy. People with heat illness often don't realize they are getting sick.
Trenches and pavement get hotter than open ground, and PPE adds heat.
ask: Where is our water and shade today?
What's the difference between heat exhaustion and heat stroke?

quick_check.scenario: A pipelayer starts acting confused and stumbling in the afternoon. He says he's fine.
quick_check.answer: Treat it as heat stroke. Get him out of the trench, call 911, and start cooling him right away. Don't let him go sit in a hot truck alone.

reference: NIOSH Criteria for a Recommended Standard: Heat Stress
State heat standards where they apply: California Title 8 CCR 3395; Washington WAC 296-62-095; Oregon OAR 437-002-0156 and 437-004-1131; Maryland COMAR 09.12.32
OSHA/NIOSH InfoSheet: Protecting Workers from Heat Illness

title: Cold Stress
why: Cold, wet and wind take heat out of your body fast. Working in wet trenches in winter can bring on hypothermia, frostbite and trench foot without much warning.
key_points: Dress in layers: a wicking base layer, an insulating layer, and a windproof and waterproof outer layer.
Keep dry. Wet clothes, wet boots and wet gloves pull heat from your body. Bring spares.
Cover your head, hands and feet. Use hard hat liners compatible with your hard hat.
Take warm breaks in a heated truck or shelter, and drink warm, sweet, non-alcoholic fluids.
Hypothermia signs: shivering, slurred speech, clumsiness, confusion. Get the person warm and dry, and get medical help.
Frostbite: numbness, white or grayish skin, usually on fingers, toes, ears and nose. Don't rub it. Get medical help.
Trench foot comes from cold, wet feet for long periods. Keep feet dry and change socks.
Ice and frost affect trench walls, footing and ladder rungs. Frozen ground can thaw and weaken during the day. Fatal Four: falls and caught-in/between — see TT-065.
ask: What's your plan to stay dry when working in a wet trench this winter?
Who watches for shivering or confusion on a cold day?

quick_check.scenario: A worker has been in a wet trench all morning, is shivering hard and fumbling with tools.
quick_check.answer: Get him out and to a warm truck, get wet clothes off, give him warm fluids and watch for worsening. Get medical help if signs continue.

title: Lightning and Storms
why: Lightning hits tall objects and open ground: excavator booms, boom trucks, and people standing in the open. Storms also bring runoff that floods trenches.
key_points: When thunder roars, go indoors. If you hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck.
Get in a building or a hard-topped metal vehicle with the windows up. A shed, open cab or tree is not safe.
Get out of the trench and away from the excavator, boom and anything tall or metal.
Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back to work.
Check the weather before the shift and keep an eye on it during the day. Use an app or radio alerts.
Heavy rain means a competent person inspects the trench before anyone goes back in.
High winds can blow over signs, barricades and portable toilets. Secure them.
Someone on site should be responsible for calling the weather stop.
ask: Where is our shelter if a storm hits right now?
Who calls the weather stop on this crew?

quick_check.scenario: Thunder rumbles in the distance. The crew wants to finish one more joint.
quick_check.answer: Stop now. Get out of the trench and into a building or hard-topped vehicle. Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.

reference: NOAA / National Weather Service lightning safety guidance

title: Cut-Off Saws and Cutting Pipe
why: Gas cut-off saws are used every day to cut pipe, concrete and pavement. They can kick back hard enough to cause serious injury, and the blades can shatter. Fatal Four: struck-by — see TT-065.
key_points: Read the saw's manual. Use the right blade for the material: ductile iron, PVC, concrete or asphalt.
Check that the blade's marked maximum RPM is equal to or higher than the saw's speed, per the saw manual. Inspect it for cracks, chips and damage before mounting.
Keep the guard in place and adjusted. Never remove it.
Kickback happens when the upper part of the blade gets pinched or hits something. Cut with the lower part of the blade, and support the pipe so the cut doesn't close on the blade.
Stand to the side of the blade, not behind it, with solid footing and both hands on the saw.
Wear eye and face protection, hearing protection, gloves and the right clothing. Cut concrete and cement-lined pipe wet, as silica Table 1 requires.
Shut off the engine and let it cool before refueling. Keep fuel away from sparks.
Never cut above shoulder height, and never use a cut-off saw from a ladder.
ask: What blade is on the saw right now, and is it rated for what we're cutting?
Where does the pipe need to be supported so it doesn't pinch the blade?

quick_check.scenario: A worker is cutting a ductile iron pipe laid on the ground with no supports. The pipe starts to close on the blade.
quick_check.answer: Stop and back off. Support the pipe on both sides so the cut opens up, not closes. A pinched blade causes kickback.

title: Hand and Power Tools, Cords and GFCI
why: Tools are used so often we stop thinking about them. Damaged cords, missing guards and wet conditions in trenches set up shocks, cuts and eye injuries. Fatal Four: electrocution — see TT-065.
key_points: Inspect tools before use. Damaged tools are tagged and removed from service.
Keep guards on power tools in place. Don't defeat safety switches.
Use GFCI protection on 120-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-amp receptacles that are not part of the permanent wiring, or follow the company's assured equipment grounding program.
Inspect cords for cuts, missing ground pins and taped repairs. Damaged cords get pulled from service.
Keep cords out of water and away from equipment travel paths. Don't run them through doorways or pinch points.
Use the right tool for the job. A wrench is not a hammer; a screwdriver is not a pry bar.
Disconnect tools before changing bits, blades or accessories.
Carry tools by the handle, never by the cord or hose.
ask: What's the condition of the cords on our trailer today?
Where are we using electric tools in wet areas?

quick_check.scenario: A pump cord has a cut in the jacket, wrapped in electrical tape, and is lying in water at the bottom of the trench.
quick_check.answer: Pull it out of service. Damaged cords don't get taped and used, especially in water. Use a good cord on GFCI protection.

title: PPE Basics
why: PPE is the last line of defense, not the first. But on a pipe job, the hard hat, boots, gloves and vest are what's between you and the next falling rock, rolling pipe or passing car. Fatal Four: struck-by — see TT-065.
key_points: Hard hats where there's a danger of head injury from falling or flying objects, including in the trench.
Safety-toe boots are standard on our jobs. Rubber boots with safety toes in wet trenches.
Gloves suited to the task: cut-resistant for pipe and saws, chemical-resistant for PVC primer and solvent cement, and waterproof gloves for live sewer work.
High-visibility vest or clothing whenever you're exposed to traffic or working around equipment.
PPE has to fit and be in good shape. Replace cracked hard hats, worn-out gloves and faded vests.
Check the manufacturer's instructions on hard hat replacement and after any impact.
Don't modify PPE: no drilling holes in hard hats, no cutting off sleeves of protective gear.
If the task changes, the PPE may change. Ask before you start a new task.
ask: What PPE does your task need today that it didn't yesterday?
Is anyone's PPE worn out and needing replacement?

quick_check.scenario: A pipelayer's hard hat took a hit from a falling clod yesterday. It looks fine.
quick_check.answer: Replace it. Follow the manufacturer's instructions; a hard hat that took a hit can be weakened even if you can't see damage.

title: Hearing and Eye Protection
why: Saws, jackhammers, compactors and engines are loud enough to cause permanent hearing loss. Cutting, grinding and chipping throw debris into eyes. Both injuries are permanent and easy to prevent.
key_points: If you have to raise your voice to talk to someone an arm's length away, it's loud enough to need hearing protection.
When noise exceeds the construction noise limits, OSHA requires feasible controls first, then hearing protection. Wear plugs or muffs around saws, jackhammers, tampers and engines.
Earplugs must be inserted right to work. Roll, pull the ear up and back, and hold the plug while it expands.
Plain cotton in your ears is not hearing protection.
Safety glasses with side protection whenever there's a chance of flying particles.
Use goggles or a face shield over safety glasses for cutting, grinding, chipping and splashes.
Eye protection must meet ANSI Z87.1. Look for the marking.
Know where the eyewash is if you work with corrosive materials.
ask: Which tasks on today's job need hearing protection?
Where is the eyewash station, and how do you use it?

quick_check.scenario: A worker running a jackhammer has his earplugs hanging around his neck because they're uncomfortable.
quick_check.answer: Put them in. Try a different size or style, or use muffs. Jackhammers are loud enough to cause permanent damage.

reference: 29 CFR 1926.101 (hearing protection; (c) plain cotton not acceptable)

title: Bypass Pumping
why: Bypass pumping keeps a live sewer flowing while we work on it. If a pump stops, a hose fails or a plug lets go, sewage backs up, overflows or floods the work area. Fatal Four: struck-by — see TT-065.
key_points: Follow the bypass plan: pump size, backup pumps, hose routes and plug locations.
Check all hose connections, clamps and couplings before starting. Secure the hoses so they can't whip.
Monitor the pumps and the upstream level for the whole time the bypass is running.
Have backup pumps ready and know how to start them.
Never stand in line with a plug or a pressurized hose connection.
Manholes and wet wells used for the bypass are confined spaces. Follow the permit system.
Fuel pumps safely, away from manholes and with spill control ready.
Know the emergency plan for an overflow: who to call, how to stop flow, and how to contain a spill.
ask: What happens if the main bypass pump fails at 2 a.m.?
Who checks the bypass during the shift, and how often?

quick_check.scenario: A bypass hose coupling is leaking slightly at a joint.
quick_check.answer: Report it and fix it before it gets worse. Leaks can turn into failures, and sewage spills must be reported per the plan.

title: Dewatering
why: Groundwater makes trench walls weak and pipe bedding unstable. Dewatering keeps the trench workable, but pumps, wellpoints and hoses bring their own hazards. Fatal Four: caught-in/between and electrocution — see TT-065.
key_points: The competent person monitors water removal equipment and operations.
If the pumps stop, water and soil conditions can change fast. Have a plan for pump failure.
Engine-driven pumps make CO. Keep them out of the trench and away from where people work.
Electric pumps need GFCI protection. Inspect cords and keep them out of the water where possible.
Discharge water where the plan says, away from the trench and in line with environmental rules.
Watch for soil being pulled out with the water. Cloudy discharge or sinkholes near the trench are warning signs.
Wellpoint and header pipes are trip hazards. Route and mark them.
Hoses under pressure can whip. Secure hoses and keep out of line with couplings.
ask: Is our discharge water clear or muddy? What does it mean?
What do we do if the dewatering stops while people are in the trench?

quick_check.scenario: The trench pump has been running all morning. A depression starts forming in the ground next to the trench.
quick_check.answer: Stop work and get people out. Soil may be getting pulled out with the water. The competent person inspects before anyone re-enters.

title: Pressure and Air Testing
why: Testing new pipe puts it under pressure. A plug, cap or fitting that lets go turns into a missile, and air under pressure stores far more energy than water. Fatal Four: struck-by — see TT-065.
key_points: Follow the test procedure and the pipe manufacturer's requirements. Test pressures and methods come from the spec, not from guesswork.
Thrust blocks and restraints must be in place, and concrete thrust blocks cured enough per the spec, before the test.
Nobody stands in front of a plug, cap or test head under pressure. Stay out of the line of fire.
Nobody in the trench or manhole near the plug during an air test.
Use a pressure gauge and a relief valve sized for the test. Don't exceed the test pressure.
Never air test PVC pressure pipe; test it with water. Do not air test any pipe the manufacturer prohibits.
Release pressure fully before removing plugs, caps or test equipment.
Brace or block plugs so they can't blow out.
ask: Where is the line of fire during today's test?
How do we know the pressure is fully released?

quick_check.scenario: During an air test on a sewer line, a worker goes into the manhole to check a plug while the line is still pressurized.
quick_check.answer: No. Release the pressure fully before anyone enters or touches the plug. A plug can blow out with enough force to kill.

reference: Pipe manufacturer's installation and testing guide
AWWA C600-23 (ductile iron mains) / AWWA C605-21 (PVC and PVCO pressure pipe)
ASTM F1417 (low-pressure air test, plastic gravity sewer); Uni-Bell: no air testing of pressure pipe

title: Slips, Trips and Falls
why: Slips, trips and falls are among the most common injuries on pipe jobs: mud, spoil, pipe on the ground, hoses and the trench edge. A fall into a trench or open manhole can be deadly. Fatal Four: falls — see TT-065.
key_points: Watch your footing on spoil, mud, wet pipe and uneven ground.
Keep walkways clear of hoses, cords, tools and pipe. Route hoses and cords out of the walkway.
Cover or barricade open manholes, pits and holes when nobody is working in them.
Walkways over trenches need guardrails if they are 6 ft or more above the lower level.
Protect the edge of excavations 6 ft or deeper with guardrails, fences or barricades where the edge is hard to see.
Three points of contact getting on and off equipment. Don't jump down.
Wear boots with good tread. Clean mud off your boots and equipment steps.
Don't carry so much that you can't see where you're walking.
ask: Where are our biggest trip hazards today?
Which open holes need covering at the end of the shift?

quick_check.scenario: At the end of the day, the crew leaves a new manhole open without a cover or barricade.
quick_check.answer: Cover it or barricade it before leaving. An open hole is a fall hazard for workers and the public.

title: Housekeeping
why: A messy site is a dangerous site. Pipe, fittings, hoses and trash lying around cause trips, hide hazards and slow down emergency response. Fatal Four: falls — see TT-065.
key_points: Keep work areas, walkways and stairs clear of debris and material.
Stack pipe and materials so they can't roll or fall. Chock pipe.
Keep the trench bottom clear of loose material and tools when not in use.
Clear form scrap from thrust blocks, collars and manhole bases. Pull or bend over nails sticking out.
Put trash in containers and get it off site regularly.
Keep fuel, oil and chemicals in their own area, away from heat and ignition sources.
Clean up as you go. Don't wait for the end of the day.
Keep the emergency access route open for an ambulance or fire truck.
ask: What part of our site needs cleanup right now?
Can an ambulance get to the trench today?

quick_check.scenario: Pipe and fittings are scattered along the trench edge, partly blocking the walkway.
quick_check.answer: Clean it up. Stack and chock the pipe at least 2 ft back from the edge and keep the walkway open.

title: Fire and Fueling
why: We carry gasoline, diesel and cutting equipment to every site. A fuel fire spreads fast. Knowing how to fuel safely and where the extinguisher is can save equipment and lives.
key_points: Shut off engines before refueling and let hot saws and pumps cool.
Use approved safety cans for gasoline and other flammable liquids, and label them.
No smoking or open flames near fueling or fuel storage.
Keep a fire extinguisher handy where fuel is used, and know where it is.
Use the extinguisher with PASS: pull the pin, aim at the base, squeeze the handle, sweep side to side.
Don't fight a fire that's spreading or blocking your exit. Get out and call 911.
Clean up spills right away and keep spill kits on site.
Hot work (cutting, welding, torches) near fuel or vegetation needs a fire watch and an extinguisher ready.
ask: Where is the nearest extinguisher to where you're working?
When was it last inspected?

quick_check.scenario: A worker refuels a hot cut-off saw with the engine still running to save time.
quick_check.answer: Stop. Shut off the engine, let it cool, then fuel away from ignition sources with a safety can.

reference: 29 CFR 1926.352 (fire prevention in welding and cutting)

title: Emergency Action and Trench Rescue
why: When someone is hurt or trapped, every minute counts. If the crew doesn't know the address, who to call or what to do, help arrives late. In a cave-in, rescuers who jump in often become the next victims. Fatal Four: caught-in/between — see TT-065.
key_points: Know the site address or nearest cross streets, and where to send the ambulance in.
Post emergency numbers on site: 911, the nearest hospital, utilities and the company's emergency contacts.
Have someone meet the emergency responders at the entrance and guide them in.
In a cave-in: call 911 right away and ask for trench rescue. Keep people and equipment away from the edge.
Do not jump into a collapsed trench. Secondary collapses are common and deadly.
Shut down nearby equipment to reduce vibration, unless it is needed by rescue.
Do not dig a buried worker out with the excavator.
Know the plan for other emergencies: utility strikes, fires, medical problems and severe weather.
ask: What is the address of this job right now?
Who meets the ambulance at the gate?

quick_check.scenario: A wall collapses and partly buries a worker. A crewmember grabs a shovel and starts to climb in.
quick_check.answer: Stop him. Call 911 for trench rescue, keep everyone back from the edge, shut down equipment and wait for trained rescuers.

reference: 29 CFR 1926.35 (emergency action plans, where a standard requires one)
29 CFR 1926.50(f) (post numbers where 911 is not available; make sure 911 works from the site)
NIOSH FACE 07NY033 (would-be rescuers and secondary collapse)

title: First Aid on the Job
why: Jobsites are often far from a hospital. A trained first aider and a stocked kit can control bleeding and keep a person alive until help arrives.
key_points: Know who on the crew is trained in first aid and CPR.
Know where the first aid kit is, and check that it's stocked.
Call 911 for serious injuries: heavy bleeding, chest pain, trouble breathing, head injuries, or loss of consciousness.
Control bleeding with direct pressure. Use a tourniquet for life-threatening limb bleeding if you're trained.
Do not move an injured person with possible neck or back injury unless they are in danger where they are.
Protect yourself from blood: wear gloves when giving first aid.
Report all injuries, even small ones, to the foreman.
Know where the nearest emergency room is and the fastest route.
ask: Who on this crew is first aid trained?
Where is the first aid kit and the AED, if we have one?

quick_check.scenario: A worker gets a deep cut on his forearm from a pipe edge and it's bleeding heavily.
quick_check.answer: Put on gloves, apply firm direct pressure, call 911 if bleeding doesn't stop, and use a tourniquet only if trained and bleeding is life-threatening.

title: Fatigue
why: Long days, early starts and hot weather wear you down. Tired workers make mistakes, miss hazards and react slowly. Fatigue on a pipe job puts everyone at risk.
key_points: Get enough sleep. Adults need at least 7 hours a night.
Long shifts and many days in a row add up. Watch for signs of fatigue in yourself and others.
Signs: yawning, slow reactions, poor focus, irritability, nodding off.
Operators: if you're nodding off, stop and tell the foreman.
Slow reactions around a swinging bucket or a backing truck can kill. Fatal Four: struck-by — see TT-065.
Take breaks, drink water and eat real food during the day.
Driving home tired is dangerous. Speak up if you're too tired to drive.
Rotate tasks when possible to reduce fatigue.
Tell the foreman if fatigue is affecting your work. It's better to say it than get hurt.
ask: How many hours did you sleep last night?
What helps you stay alert on long days?

quick_check.scenario: An operator is yawning, missing signals and slow to react after a long week of overtime.
quick_check.answer: He tells the foreman, takes a break or switches tasks. Fatigue is a hazard, not a toughness test.

reference: NIOSH work schedules and fatigue guidance; CDC (AASM/SRS: at least 7 hours for adults 18-60)

title: Respect and Communication
why: Crews that trust each other speak up about hazards. Yelling, joking at someone's expense or ignoring people shuts down communication and makes people stay quiet when it matters.
key_points: Treat everyone on the crew with respect, including new workers, subcontractors and inspectors.
Speak clearly and confirm that the message was understood. Use repeat-back for critical instructions.
Agree on hand signals and radio calls before work starts.
No harassment, hazing or bullying. Report it.
Language barriers: make sure safety instructions are understood by everyone, in a language they understand.
Listen when someone raises a concern. They may see something you don't.
Give credit when someone catches a hazard. That's how people keep speaking up.
Handle disagreements off the work area, not in the trench or near equipment.
ask: How do we make sure new workers understand our signals?
What makes it hard to speak up on a crew?

quick_check.scenario: A new worker who speaks limited English nods during the briefing but looks unsure.
quick_check.answer: Check understanding: show him the hand signals, use someone who speaks his language, and confirm he knows the plan.

reference: OSHA training policy: instruction in a language and vocabulary workers understand

title: Suicide in Construction: The Numbers
why: We talk every week about cave-ins, struck-by and utility strikes. But in our industry, suicide kills far more workers than job-site injuries do. These are our brothers and sisters, and suicide is preventable. Help works.
key_points: In 2021, CDC found men in the construction industry died by suicide at 56.0 per 100,000. For all working men, the rate was 32.0.
Men in construction and extraction jobs, which covers most of us, had a rate of 65.6 per 100,000 in 2021, one of the highest of any occupation group.
In 2021, construction was 7.4% of the workforce but 17.9% of suicide deaths where the industry was known. More than 5,000 construction workers died by suicide that year (CPWR).
NIOSH found the suicide rate for men in construction jobs was about 5 times the rate of all fatal work injuries in construction (2016 and 2018 data).
There is no single cause. Long hours, pain, time away from home, money and a 'just deal with it' culture can all stack up.
Most people who have thought about suicide get through it. Support, coping skills and treatment work for most of them.
This crew watches each other's backs on the job. That includes this.

If you or someone on the crew is struggling, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), any time. In an emergency, call 911. Ask your foreman about your company's Employee Assistance Program (EAP).
ask: Did any of these numbers surprise you? Why do you think our trade is hit so hard?
Do you know where to find our EAP number, and is it posted on this job?

quick_check.scenario: A laborer says, 'That stuff doesn't happen on crews like ours.'
quick_check.answer: It can happen on any crew. Construction has one of the highest suicide rates of any industry. That is why we look out for each other and know the 988 number.
