reference: CDC MMWR 2023;72(50):1346-1350, Suicide Rates by Industry and Occupation, United States, 2021 data
CPWR, Suicides Among Construction Workers in the United States, 2021 (Am J Ind Med, 2025)
NIOSH Science Blog, Partnering to Prevent Suicide in the Construction Industry
OSHA Publication 4446, Suicide Prevention in Construction: 5 Things You Should Know (2024)

title: Warning Signs in a Coworker
why: You spend more waking hours with this crew than with your family. You are often the first to notice when someone is not right. Most people who die by suicide show at least one warning sign in what they say or do.
key_points: Watch for talk about being a burden, feeling trapped, having no reason to live, feeling hopeless, being in unbearable pain, or wanting to die.
Watch for changes in behavior: drinking or using more, pulling away from the crew, sleeping too much or too little, giving away prized things, or saying goodbye.
Watch for mood changes: depression, anxiety, losing interest, irritability, anger, shame, or a sudden calm after a hard stretch.
Changes matter most when they follow a loss, a breakup, a divorce, an injury, a layoff or legal trouble.
Changes on the job count too: showing up late, missing days, careless work, near misses, short temper.
You do not need to be sure. If something seems off, check in. It is better to ask and be wrong than to stay quiet.
If someone talks about wanting to die, take it seriously every time, even if it sounds like a joke.

If you or someone on the crew is struggling, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), any time. In an emergency, call 911. Ask your foreman about your company's Employee Assistance Program (EAP).
ask: What would you notice first if one of us was having a hard time?
Have you ever wished someone had checked in on you?

quick_check.scenario: A pipelayer who is usually the loudest guy on the crew has gone quiet for two weeks. He says, 'Doesn't matter, nobody would miss me anyway.'
quick_check.answer: That is a warning sign. Find a private moment, ask how he is really doing, and ask directly if he is thinking about suicide. Then connect him to help: 988, the EAP, or a doctor.

reference: American Foundation for Suicide Prevention (AFSP), warning signs and 'ask directly' guidance
OSHA Publication 4446, Suicide Prevention in Construction: 5 Things You Should Know (2024)
CDC, Risk and Protective Factors for Suicide (cdc.gov/suicide)

title: Starting the Conversation: "Are You OK?"
why: Most of us are scared of saying the wrong thing, so we say nothing. You do not need the perfect words. Showing that you noticed and that you care can be the thing that opens the door.
key_points: Pick a private moment: the truck, the walk to the spoil pile, after shift. Not in front of the crew.
Say what you have seen: 'You've seemed off lately. You're not yourself. What's going on?'
Ask twice. The first answer is usually 'I'm fine.' Try 'No, really. How are you doing?'
Listen more than you talk. Let silences happen. You do not need to fix it or have an answer.
Do not judge, argue or lecture. Skip 'You've got it good' or 'Just snap out of it.'
Thank them for telling you. Tell them they matter to you and to this crew.
If what you hear worries you, ask about suicide directly and connect them to help (next talks).

If you or someone on the crew is struggling, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), any time. In an emergency, call 911. Ask your foreman about your company's Employee Assistance Program (EAP).
ask: What is one line you could use to check on someone that sounds like you?
What makes it hard to say 'I'm not OK' on a crew?

quick_check.scenario: You ask a coworker how he's doing. He says, 'Fine,' but he has been missing days and snapping at people.
quick_check.answer: Ask again in private and name what you have seen: 'You've been off for a while. I'm not going anywhere. What's going on?' Then listen without trying to fix it.

reference: OSHA Publication 4446, Suicide Prevention in Construction: 5 Things You Should Know (2024)
American Foundation for Suicide Prevention (AFSP), warning signs and 'ask directly' guidance
Construction Industry Alliance for Suicide Prevention (preventconstructionsuicide.com)

title: Asking Directly About Suicide
why: Many people worry that asking about suicide will put the idea in someone's head. It will not. Research shows asking directly does not make people suicidal and can actually help. A straight question shows you can handle the answer.
key_points: Ask plainly and calmly: 'Are you thinking about suicide?' or 'Are you thinking about killing yourself?'
Do not ask in a way that wants a 'no', like 'You're not thinking of doing something stupid, are you?'
Many people feel relief when someone finally asks. It means they don't have to hide it.
If the answer is yes, stay calm. Thank them for being honest. Do not leave them alone.
Ask if they are safe right now. If they are in immediate danger, call 911.
Do not promise to keep it a secret. Their life is more important than a secret.
Then connect them to help together: call or text 988 with them, or get them to the EAP or a doctor.

If you or someone on the crew is struggling, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), any time. In an emergency, call 911. Ask your foreman about your company's Employee Assistance Program (EAP).
ask: Why do you think people avoid asking this question?
Could you say the question out loud right now, just to practice?

quick_check.scenario: A coworker tells you he can't see a way out and everyone would be better off without him. You are afraid asking will make it worse.
quick_check.answer: Ask directly: 'Are you thinking about suicide?' Asking will not put the idea in his head. If he says yes, stay with him and call or text 988 together. If he is in immediate danger, call 911.

reference: American Foundation for Suicide Prevention (AFSP), warning signs and 'ask directly' guidance
Dazzi T. et al., Psychological Medicine 2014;44(16):3361-3363 (asking about suicide does not induce suicidal ideation)
OSHA Publication 4446, Suicide Prevention in Construction: 5 Things You Should Know (2024)

title: Getting Someone to Help
why: You are not their counselor. Your job is to get them to people who are trained to help, and not to let go until they are connected. Help works. Most people who have thought about suicide get through it with support and treatment.
key_points: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: call or text 988, or chat at chat.988lifeline.org. It is free, confidential and open 24/7.
988 has Spanish (press 2, or text AYUDA to 988). Veterans and service members can press 1. Deaf and hard of hearing callers can use 988 Videophone, or 711 then 988 by TTY.
Make the call or text together. Sit with them while they talk, or offer to dial and hand them the phone.
Company EAP: usually free and confidential counseling for workers and family. Ask the foreman or office for the number.
A family doctor can also help, and can treat depression, anxiety, pain and sleep problems.
If they are in immediate danger, call 911 and stay with them until help arrives. Help put time and distance between them and anything they could use to hurt themselves.
Follow up in the next few days. 'Hey, how did it go?' matters more than you think.

If you or someone on the crew is struggling, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), any time. In an emergency, call 911. Ask your foreman about your company's Employee Assistance Program (EAP).
ask: Who on this crew has 988 saved in their phone? Do it now.
Where is our EAP number posted?

quick_check.scenario: At the end of the shift a coworker tells you he has been thinking about suicide. He asks you not to tell anyone and says he'll be fine tomorrow.
quick_check.answer: Do not leave him alone or keep it secret. Stay with him and call or text 988 together. If he is in immediate danger, call 911. Let the foreman know quietly, not the whole crew, and check on him again tomorrow.

reference: SAMHSA, In Crisis? Call or Text 988 (samhsa.gov)
OSHA Publication 4446, Suicide Prevention in Construction: 5 Things You Should Know (2024)

title: Long Hours, Travel and Time Away from Home
why: Sixty-hour weeks, motel rooms, missed birthdays and long drives are part of pipeline work. They wear on you and on the people at home. CDC lists long work hours and job stress among the work factors that can raise suicide risk.
key_points: Stress builds slowly. Short temper, poor sleep, more drinking and pulling away are signs it is building.
Being far from home can mean being cut off. Feeling connected to people is one of the strongest protections there is.
Stay in touch with home every day if you can, even a two-minute call or a video.
On the road, don't just go back to the room alone every night. Eat with the crew. Check on the new guy.
Use the time off you get. Rest is part of doing this job for a long career.
If overtime is wearing you down, talk to the foreman. Saying so is not weakness.
Your EAP can usually help family at home too, not just you.

If you or someone on the crew is struggling, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), any time. In an emergency, call 911. Ask your foreman about your company's Employee Assistance Program (EAP).
ask: What helps you stay connected to home when we're on the road?
Who on this crew is far from home right now and could use a check-in?

quick_check.scenario: A new hand is three states from home on his first travel job. He eats alone, skips crew dinners and says his girlfriend stopped calling.
quick_check.answer: Invite him in. Eat with him, ask how he is really doing, and make sure he knows about the EAP and 988. Being cut off is a real risk, and a crew can fix part of it.

reference: NIOSH Science Blog, Critical Steps Your Workplace Can Take Today to Prevent Suicide (2023)
CDC, Risk and Protective Factors for Suicide (cdc.gov/suicide)
CPWR, Suicides Among Construction Workers in the United States, 2021 (Am J Ind Med, 2025)

title: Sleep and Your Mental Health
why: Poor sleep and poor mental health feed each other. Bad nights make stress, anger and low moods worse, and stress makes it hard to sleep. On a pipe job, a tired mind is also a safety hazard. (See also TT-051 Fatigue.)
key_points: NIOSH says most adults need 7 to 8 hours of quality sleep a night.
Being awake 17 hours is like a blood alcohol level of 0.05%. Being awake 24 hours is like 0.10%, above the legal limit for driving (NIOSH).
Don't drink any alcohol when you're short on sleep and need to drive or do critical work. It makes the impairment worse.
Using alcohol to fall asleep, or energy drinks to get through the day, can turn into a cycle that is hard to break.
Sleeping much more or much less than usual can be a warning sign of depression or of someone who is struggling.
Sleep problems that last for weeks are worth taking to a doctor. Many are treatable.
Protect the sleep you can: dark room, phone down, same wake-up time when possible.
A tired mind is slow to spot a swinging bucket or a backing truck. Fatal Four: struck-by — see TT-065.

If you or someone on the crew is struggling, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), any time. In an emergency, call 911. Ask your foreman about your company's Employee Assistance Program (EAP).
ask: What gets in the way of your sleep on this job?
Have you noticed your mood change after a few short nights?

quick_check.scenario: An operator says he has been sleeping about four hours a night for weeks because his mind won't shut off. He's been drinking to knock himself out.
quick_check.answer: That is more than being tired. Talk with him privately, encourage him to see a doctor or call the EAP, and make sure he knows about 988. Tell the foreman if he is too tired to run equipment safely.

reference: NIOSH, Work Schedules: Shift Work and Long Work Hours, Sleep and Fatigue training module
NIOSH, Impaired performance from lack of sleep (BAC comparison)
American Foundation for Suicide Prevention (AFSP), warning signs and 'ask directly' guidance

title: Alcohol, Drugs and Getting Through
why: Lots of people use alcohol or drugs to cope with pain or stress. That is not a character flaw, but it can get out of hand. In 2020, CDC found construction and extraction workers had the highest drug overdose death rate of any occupation group: 162.6 per 100,000, against 42.1 for all workers.
key_points: In 2008 to 2012 survey data, 16.5% of full-time construction workers reported heavy drinking in the past month, and 14.3% had a substance use disorder in the past year (SAMHSA).
Needing more to get through the day, or not being able to stop when you want to, is worth talking about.
Opioids after an injury: take them only as prescribed, never share or sell them, store them safely, and ask the pharmacist how to get rid of leftovers. Ask your doctor about other pain options.
Naloxone (Narcan) can reverse an opioid overdose. It is sold over the counter without a prescription. Keep it with the first aid kit, stored as the package says.
Signs of overdose: won't wake up or respond, shallow or no breathing, pinpoint pupils. Call 911, give naloxone if you have it, and don't leave them alone.
SAMHSA National Helpline: 1-800-662-4357. Free, confidential, 24/7 treatment referral in English and Spanish. Also FindTreatment.gov.
Getting help is a safety decision, not a confession. Talk to the EAP or a doctor.

If you or someone on the crew is struggling, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), any time. In an emergency, call 911. Ask your foreman about your company's Employee Assistance Program (EAP).
ask: Do we have naloxone on this job? Where is it?
What would make it easier for someone here to ask for help with drinking or drugs?

quick_check.scenario: A coworker hurt his back last year and is still taking pain pills. He's been buying extra from someone, and he nods off in the truck.
quick_check.answer: Talk to him privately without judging. Tell him you're worried and encourage him to see his doctor or call the EAP or 1-800-662-4357. Keep him off equipment while impaired, and know where the naloxone is.

reference: CDC NCHS QuickStats, Drug Overdose Death Rates Among Workers by Usual Occupation, 2020 data (MMWR 2022)
SAMHSA, Substance Use and Substance Use Disorder by Industry (2015; NSDUH 2008-2012)
FDA, approval of OTC naloxone nasal spray (March 29, 2023)
CDC Rx Awareness, Prevent opioid overdose (signs, naloxone, safe storage)
CPWR, Overdose Fatalities at Worksites and Opioid Use in the Construction Industry (2020)

title: Chronic Pain, Injury and Your Head
why: Bad backs, shoulders and knees come with years in the trench. Living with pain every day wears down your patience, your sleep and your mood. CDC lists serious illness such as chronic pain among the risk factors for suicide. CPWR researchers point to work injuries and chronic pain as one reason construction is hit so hard.
key_points: Pain and low mood often travel together. Feeling down, angry or hopeless when you're hurting is common, and it is treatable.
An injury can take away more than your body: your paycheck, your routine, your crew and your sense of who you are.
Report injuries early and get them looked at. Pain that is treated early is easier to manage than pain that's been pushed through for years.
Tell your doctor about your mood and sleep, not just the pain. They're connected.
Ask about all your options: physical therapy, stretching, light duty, and pain treatment that isn't only pills.
If a coworker is off injured, stay in touch. A call or a visit tells him he's still part of the crew.

If you or someone on the crew is struggling, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), any time. In an emergency, call 911. Ask your foreman about your company's Employee Assistance Program (EAP).
ask: Who here is working through pain right now? You don't have to say it out loud, but think about whether you've told a doctor.
How do we keep in touch with crew members who are off injured?

quick_check.scenario: A pipelayer has been on light duty for two months with a shoulder injury. He says, 'What good am I if I can't do the work?' and has stopped coming to lunch.
quick_check.answer: That's a warning sign. Check in privately, tell him he still matters to the crew, and ask directly how bad it's gotten. Encourage him to talk to his doctor about mood as well as pain, and share the EAP and 988.

reference: CDC, Risk and Protective Factors for Suicide (cdc.gov/suicide)
CPWR, Suicides Among Construction Workers in the United States, 2021 (Am J Ind Med, 2025)
CPWR, Overdose Fatalities at Worksites and Opioid Use in the Construction Industry (2020)

title: Toughness and Asking for Help
why: Our trade is built on being tough. Work through it, don't complain, handle your own problems. That toughness gets the pipe in the ground. But CDC lists stigma about asking for help as a risk factor for suicide. Keeping quiet doesn't make the problem go away.
key_points: You'd never let a guy go into an unprotected trench to look tough. Mental health is the same: you use the protection that's there.
Asking for help is a strength. It takes more guts to say 'I'm not OK' than to keep faking it.
You'd see a doctor for a broken arm. Depression, anxiety and stress are health problems too, and treatment works.
Watch what we joke about. Jokes about being 'weak' or 'crazy' teach people to stay quiet.
Leaders go first. When a foreman or a veteran hand talks about a hard time they've had, it makes it OK for everyone else.
EAPs are set up to be confidential. Ask how ours works. It's there so you can get help without the whole job knowing.

If you or someone on the crew is struggling, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), any time. In an emergency, call 911. Ask your foreman about your company's Employee Assistance Program (EAP).
ask: What would you think of a coworker who asked for help? Would you think less of him? Then why think less of yourself?
What can this crew do so that people feel OK speaking up?

quick_check.scenario: A crew member mentions he's been seeing a counselor. Someone cracks, 'What, you going soft?' and the crew laughs.
quick_check.answer: Shut that down. Say, 'That took guts, good for him.' Stigma is a real risk factor. A crew that backs people who get help makes it safer for everyone to speak up.

reference: CDC, Risk and Protective Factors for Suicide (cdc.gov/suicide)
CPWR, Suicides Among Construction Workers in the United States, 2021 (Am J Ind Med, 2025)
Construction Industry Alliance for Suicide Prevention (preventconstructionsuicide.com)
NIOSH Science Blog, Critical Steps Your Workplace Can Take Today to Prevent Suicide (2023)

title: Money Stress and Seasonal Layoffs
why: Construction work goes up and down with the season and the bids. One month it's overtime, the next you're laid off waiting for the call. CDC lists job or financial problems or loss among the risk factors for suicide. Money stress is common, and there are ways through it.
key_points: Seasonal or uneven work is one of the work factors CPWR researchers point to in construction.
Money stress usually travels with other things: fights at home, poor sleep, drinking more. Watch for those.
Plan for the slow season while the checks are big. Even a small cushion takes some pressure off.
Ask whether your EAP offers financial or legal counseling. Some do, and it's confidential.
Getting laid off cuts you off from the crew too. Keep in touch with guys who are out of work.
A layoff is not a measure of what you're worth. It's the job, not you.

If you or someone on the crew is struggling, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), any time. In an emergency, call 911. Ask your foreman about your company's Employee Assistance Program (EAP).
ask: What helps you get through the slow months?
When someone gets laid off, how could we stay in touch with them?

quick_check.scenario: The job is winding down. A laborer with two kids says he's behind on rent, isn't sleeping, and keeps saying, 'I don't know how I'm going to get out of this.'
quick_check.answer: Listen and take him seriously. Ask how he is really doing, and ask directly about suicide if you're worried. Point him to the EAP for money and family help, and make sure he has 988. Keep checking in after the layoff.

reference: CDC, Risk and Protective Factors for Suicide (cdc.gov/suicide)
CPWR, Suicides Among Construction Workers in the United States, 2021 (Am J Ind Med, 2025)
CDC NIOSH, Suicide and Occupation (job security, low pay and job stress)

title: After a Bad Day: Serious Incidents and Close Calls
why: A cave-in, a utility strike, a coworker hurt or killed, or a near miss that should have killed someone. Days like that stay with you. Feeling shaken afterwards is a normal reaction to something that isn't normal. It doesn't mean you're weak or that something is wrong with you.
key_points: Common reactions (NIOSH): trouble sleeping, nightmares, poor focus, irritability, anger, guilt, replaying it in your head, feeling numb or overwhelmed, drinking more.
For many people these reactions ease with time. If they last several weeks or get in the way of daily life, get help from a professional.
Look after the basics: eat, sleep, drink water, take breaks and keep moving. Avoid using alcohol or drugs to cope.
Talk about it with someone you trust. Reach out. People really do care.
Watch out for each other in the days after, especially anyone who saw it up close or blames himself.
Ask the company about a debrief or counselor after a serious incident. Your EAP can help.
Close calls count. You don't need someone to get hurt to have a hard reaction.

If you or someone on the crew is struggling, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), any time. In an emergency, call 911. Ask your foreman about your company's Employee Assistance Program (EAP).
ask: After something bad happens on a job, what has helped you?
Who should we check on after a serious incident?

quick_check.scenario: A week after a trench wall came down and nearly caught a coworker, the operator who was digging can't sleep and keeps saying it was his fault.
quick_check.answer: Check on him privately and let him talk. Tell him his reaction is normal. Encourage him to use the EAP, and make sure he knows about 988. If it hasn't eased after a few weeks or he's struggling to get through the day, help him see a professional.

reference: NIOSH, Traumatic Incident Stress: Information for Emergency Response Workers (Pub. 2002-107)
OSHA Publication 4446, Suicide Prevention in Construction: 5 Things You Should Know (2024)

title: The Fatal Four: What Kills Construction Workers
why: Four kinds of accidents kill more construction workers than anything else: falls, struck-by, electrocution and caught-in/between. OSHA builds its construction safety training around them and calls them the "Focus Four." Many crews know them as the Fatal Four. All four are on a pipe job every day.
key_points: OSHA's construction training names the four leading causes of fatalities on construction sites: falls, caught-in or -between, struck-by and electrocution.
In 2024, 1,034 workers in the private construction industry died from work injuries (BLS). Falls, slips and trips killed 389 of them, more than 1 in 3.

The same year, 52 construction workers died from exposure to electricity, and 161 from contact with objects and equipment: struck by, caught in or crushed, including trench and other collapses. Together with falls, that is more than half of all construction deaths.
Falls on our jobs: into trenches, pits and open manholes, off equipment and trucks, and off ladders (TT-066, TT-046, TT-007).
Struck-by: excavators, loaders, dump trucks, traffic, suspended pipe and structures, and falling or flying material (TT-069, TT-020 to TT-023, TT-026, TT-027, TT-071, TT-031 to TT-033).
Electrocution: buried and overhead power lines, cords, pumps and temporary power (TT-067, TT-011 to TT-014, TT-040).
Caught-in/between: trench cave-ins, counterweights, pinch points and moving parts (TT-068, TT-002 to TT-010, TT-024, TT-025).
Beyond the Fatal Four: suicide takes more construction workers' lives than all on-the-job fatal injuries combined. See TT-070 and the mental health talks, TT-053 to TT-064.

If you or someone on the crew is struggling, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), any time. In an emergency, call 911. Ask your foreman about your company's Employee Assistance Program (EAP).
ask: Which of the four is closest to us on today's job, and what is protecting us from it?
Who on this crew would you call if you were having a hard week?

quick_check.scenario: A new hand asks why the crew spends so much time on the trench box, spotters and the 811 ticket when 'nothing ever happens here.'
quick_check.answer: Those controls are aimed straight at the Fatal Four. Cave-ins, equipment, buried lines and falls into the trench are how pipelayers get killed. Nothing happens because the controls are in place.

reference: BLS Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries, 2024 data (released Feb. 19, 2026), Tables A-1 and A-9
OSHA Training Institute, Construction Focus Four (Introduction)
OSHA Outreach Training Program, Construction Industry Procedures (2024): Focus Four Hazards

title: Falls on a Pipeline Job
why: Falls kill more construction workers than any other cause. We rarely work on roofs, but we work beside open trenches, pits and manholes, climb on and off machines all day, and use ladders in the hole. Fatal Four: falls — see TT-065.
key_points: Excavation edges: OSHA requires each employee "at the edge of an excavation 6 feet (1.8 m) or more in depth" to be protected from falling by guardrails, fences or barricades when the excavation is not readily seen because of plant growth or another visual barrier.
Wells, pits, shafts and similar excavations 6 ft or more deep, like bore pits, wet wells and manhole holes: protect the edge with guardrails, fences, barricades or covers.
Cover or barricade open holes before the crew leaves at night. Cones alone are not a barricade.
"Walkways shall be provided where employees or equipment are required or permitted to cross over excavations." Walkways 6 ft or more above the lower level need guardrails.
Never jump a trench or cross on the pipe, the box or the spreaders.
Getting on and off equipment and trucks: face the machine and use three points of contact (two hands and a foot, or one hand and two feet). Never jump down. Clean mud off steps and handholds.
Ladders: rails at least 3 ft above the landing, on stable, level footing or secured, face the ladder, keep at least one hand on it, and don't carry a load that can make you lose balance.
Never stand on the top step of a stepladder. Use a ladder only for what it was designed for, and tag damaged ones 'Do Not Use.'
ask: Where on this job could someone fall into an excavation, and is it guarded or covered?
How do you get down from the cab or off a truck bed?

quick_check.scenario: At the end of shift, a 7 ft deep bore pit beside the sidewalk has only a few cones around it.
quick_check.answer: Not enough. A pit 6 ft or deeper needs guardrails, fencing, barricades or a cover. Cover or fence it before anyone leaves.

reference: NIOSH Pub. 2023-137, Preventing Dump Truck-related Injuries and Deaths During Construction (three points of contact)
BLS Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries, 2024 data (released Feb. 19, 2026), Tables A-1 and A-9

title: Electrocution on a Pipeline Job
why: Electricity gives no warning. On a pipe job it comes from three places: buried lines in the dig, overhead lines above the boom, and the cords, pumps and temporary power we bring ourselves. In 2024, 52 construction workers died from exposure to electricity (BLS). Fatal Four: electrocution — see TT-065.
key_points: Before work starts, the employer must find out whether any energized circuit, "exposed or concealed," could be contacted, post warning signs, and tell the crew where the lines are and how to stay safe.
Buried electric (red marks): call 811 and wait the time your state requires. The line can be anywhere inside your state's tolerance zone around the mark (TT-011).
Inside the tolerance zone, find the line by hand digging or vacuum excavation. No mechanical digging unless state law and the facility owner allow it (TT-012).
Where the exact location of buried power lines is unknown, workers using jackhammers, bars or other hand tools that could hit a line must be given insulated protective gloves.
Overhead lines: keep the boom, bucket, dump bed and load at least 10 ft from lines rated 50 kV or less, more for higher voltage, and use a spotter (TT-014).
If a machine contacts a line, the operator stays in the cab unless there is a fire. Everyone else stays clear (TT-013).
Temporary power: 120-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-amp receptacles need GFCI protection, or the company's assured equipment grounding program. Pull damaged cords (TT-040).
Pumps and dewatering: GFCI or assured grounding on cord-and-plug pumps, cords and connections out of the water, and unplug or lock out before pulling or working on a pump (TT-044, TT-025).
ask: Where are the power lines on this job, above and below?
How is our pump power protected today?

quick_check.scenario: The locate shows a red line crossing 3 ft ahead of the bucket. The operator wants one more scoop to 'find it faster.'
quick_check.answer: Stop the bucket. Inside the tolerance zone the line is found by hand or vacuum excavation. A bucket into a buried power line can energize the machine and the ground around it.

reference: OSHA FS-3941 (equipment contact with power lines)
BLS Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries, 2024 data (released Feb. 19, 2026), Tables A-1 and A-9

title: Caught-In/Between: Cave-Ins, Pinch Points and Moving Parts
why: Caught-in/between means being buried, crushed or pulled in: a trench wall letting go, getting pinned between a machine and something solid, or clothing caught in a turning part. On pipe jobs, the cave-in is the big one. Fatal Four: caught-in/between — see TT-065.
key_points: In 2024, 13 construction workers died in trench or excavation collapses (BLS). A cave-in gives you no time to climb out.

A trench 5 ft or deeper needs sloping, benching, shoring or a box before anyone gets in, unless it is entirely in stable rock. At 20 ft or deeper, a registered professional engineer designs it (TT-002, TT-004, TT-005).
The competent person inspects daily, and again after rain or anything that changes conditions. Know the warning signs (TT-003, TT-008, TT-009).
Spoil, pipe and equipment at least 2 ft back from the edge (TT-006). Stay inside the box while laying pipe (TT-010).
Never stand between the counterweight and a truck, pipe stack, wall or box. Keep hands out of joints and from between pipe and the box (TT-021, TT-024).
Moving parts: guards stay on, and no loose clothing, rings or long hair near belts, shafts and pump drives.
Before working on or under a machine: lower it, shut it down, lock it out and block anything raised (TT-025).
ask: Where on today's job could someone get buried or pinned?
Who is our competent person today?

quick_check.scenario: A joint won't seat, so a laborer reaches in between the bell and the box wall to guide it while the operator pushes.
quick_check.answer: Stop. That is a caught-between. Hands stay out of the gap. Guide with a bar or tag line from a safe spot, and agree with the operator before any push.

reference: BLS Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries, 2024 data (released Feb. 19, 2026), Tables A-1 and A-9

title: Struck-By: Equipment, Vehicles and Loads
why: Struck-by means something moving hits you: a machine, a truck, a car through the work zone, a swinging pipe, or something falling or flying. On pipe jobs we are on foot around heavy iron and traffic all day. Fatal Four: struck-by — see TT-065.
key_points: In 2024, 79 construction workers died when struck by falling, flying or swinging objects, and 67 were pedestrians hit by vehicles, 30 of them in road work zones (BLS).
Excavators and loaders: eye contact before you enter, stay out of blind spots, and respect the swing radius (TT-020, TT-021).
Trucks: no backing with a blocked rear view unless the backup alarm works or a spotter signals. Spotters stay in the mirror, never behind (TT-022).
Traffic: high-visibility gear, follow the traffic control plan, and stay inside the cones (TT-031 to TT-033).
Suspended loads: "No employee shall be permitted underneath loads handled by lifting or digging equipment." Use tag lines and rated rigging (TT-026, TT-027, TT-071).
Falling objects: hard hats on, spoil and tools back from the edge, and stand away from trucks being loaded.
Flying objects: test plugs, pressurized hoses and cut-off saws. Stay out of the line of fire (TT-023, TT-039, TT-045).
ask: What on today's job could hit someone, and where should we stand instead?
Who spots for the trucks today?

quick_check.scenario: A laborer stands in the trench right under a stick of pipe as the excavator lowers it, to guide it by hand.
quick_check.answer: Get out from under it. Guide the pipe with a tag line from a safe spot and stay clear until it is lowered into place.

reference: BLS Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries, 2024 data (released Feb. 19, 2026), Tables A-1 and A-9

title: Beyond the Fatal Four: Suicide
why: The Fatal Four are how construction workers die from on-the-job injuries. But suicide takes more construction workers' lives than all on-the-job fatal injuries combined. Suicide is preventable, and help works.
key_points: NIOSH found the suicide rate for men in construction jobs was about 5 times the rate of all fatal work injuries in construction (2016 and 2018 data).
In 2021, CDC found men in the construction industry died by suicide at 56.0 per 100,000. For all working men, the rate was 32.0.
There is no single cause. Pain, long hours, time away from home, money worries and a 'just deal with it' culture can stack up.
Most people who have thought about suicide get through it. Support, coping skills and treatment work for most of them.
We watch each other's backs for cave-ins and swinging loads. Watch for a coworker who isn't himself, too, and ask.

The mental health talks cover the numbers (TT-053), warning signs (TT-054), starting the conversation (TT-055), asking directly (TT-056) and getting someone to help (TT-057). TT-058 to TT-064 cover hours, sleep, alcohol and drugs, pain, toughness, money and bad days.

If you or someone on the crew is struggling, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), any time. In an emergency, call 911. Ask your foreman about your company's Employee Assistance Program (EAP).
ask: Who on this crew would you call if you were having a hard week?
How can we check on each other without making a big deal of it?

quick_check.scenario: After the Fatal Four talk, a coworker who has been quiet and keeping to himself for weeks jokes that 'the only thing that will kill me on this job is the overtime.'
quick_check.answer: Don't let it slide. Later, in private, tell him what you have noticed and ask how he is really doing. Listen. If you are worried, ask directly about suicide and help him connect with 988 or the EAP (TT-055, TT-056).

reference: NIOSH Science Blog, Partnering to Prevent Suicide in the Construction Industry
CDC MMWR 2023;72(50):1346-1350, Suicide Rates by Industry and Occupation, United States, 2021 data
OSHA Publication 4446, Suicide Prevention in Construction: 5 Things You Should Know (2024)

title: Setting Manholes, Vaults and Precast Structures
why: Manhole bases, barrels, cones, grade rings and vaults are the heaviest picks on most pipe jobs, and they go into a hole where people work. Fatal Four: struck-by and caught-in/between — see TT-065.
key_points: Get the weight from the precaster's ticket or drawing and check it against the excavator's lifting capacity chart at the reach you need. If it's over the chart, use a bigger machine or a crane.
Lift only with the precaster's lifting inserts or anchors and the lifting hardware they specify. Check inserts for cracks, spalls and damage before hooking up.

Use rigging rated for the load, with legs long enough. The flatter the sling, the more load on each leg: at 30 degrees from horizontal, each leg of a two-leg sling carries the full weight of the load.
Use the sling angle, spreader or lifting device the precaster calls for.

Clear the crew out of the trench and the hole before a structure goes in. OSHA: "No employee shall be permitted under precast concrete members being lifted or tilted into position except those employees required for the erection of those members."
Never ride a load, the bucket or a structure into or out of the hole.
Steady the piece with tag lines from the surface. Go in only when it is low and under control, and keep hands off the bearing surfaces while it sets.
Set it on a prepared, level base, and don't unhook until it is down and stable.
One signal person, signals agreed before the lift. Anyone can call stop.
ask: What's the heaviest structure we set this week, and what does the lift chart say at that reach?
Where does everyone stand when the base goes in?

quick_check.scenario: A vault is swinging a little as it's lowered, and a laborer in the hole reaches up to steady it by hand.
quick_check.answer: Get out from under it and out of the hole. Steady it with a tag line from the surface. Nobody under a load, and the crew stays clear until the structure is down.

reference: 29 CFR 1926.704(c)-(e) (precast lifting inserts, hardware, no one under)
29 CFR 1926.1400(c)(2) (excavators lifting with rigging are outside Subpart CC)
